answers.answer: They share a family because SCOPe groups domains by common ancestry and a shared structural architecture, not by chain length. a.298.1.1 (class a, all-alpha; fold a.298 TAL effector-like; superfamily a.298.1; family a.298.1.1 TAL effector) is a tandem-repeat domain. Each repeat is about 34 residues and folds as a helix–loop–helix hairpin. Successive repeats stack into a right-handed superhelix that wraps around the DNA major groove. Because the unit is repeated, domain length depends mostly on how many repeats a given entry or construct contains. One entry may be a short fragment or a small array. Another may be a long, near-full DNA-binding array, possibly with flanking N-/C-terminal segments. An array of about 34×n residues has a different total length from one with a different n, yet every repeat has the same local fold and the same connectivity. The homology call rests on the conserved ~34-residue repeat scaffold and superhelical packing, plus the conserved sequence pattern of the repeats. Total length does not enter into it. The family-level assignment also reflects that these are all TALE-type DNA-binding repeat proteins, mostly from Xanthomonas (some engineered or designed variants). Among them the repeats are close sequence homologs apart from the hypervariable positions. The limits are these. (1) Sharing a family does not mean sharing DNA specificity. Specificity comes mainly from the repeat-variable di-residue (RVD) at positions 12–13 of each repeat, so the order of RVDs, not family membership, decides which DNA sequence is recognized. Do not transfer a binding site or target from one entry to another by SCOPe family alone. (2) Do not use a different repeat count as evidence for a different fold or family. Equally, do not treat a longer or shorter chain as a better template. Choose a template or representative by repeat number, RVD composition, ligand state (DNA-bound or free), and construct boundaries.
